Regarding the question of whether those not included in either of the two categories are of sharp or dull faculties, and whether they are obstructed or unobstructed, the answer states:
"This refers to the four teachings. This means those who hear both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna within the Vaipulya (Fangdeng) and Prajñāpāramitā (Bore) teachings.

Since one cannot enter therein, waiting until the two types of *sneha* (clarified butter) is considered duller than the former; it is merely called "dull" because of the waiting period. Although it is duller compared to the former, once entry is attained here, its sharpness or dullness is self-evident.

Among the four gates, each subsequent gate is superior to the preceding one; therefore, among the four gates, when the fourth gate is moved to the front, it is intended to place the most excellent of the four faculties at the head. One should know that the "large" and "small" herein are no different from the "large" and "small" in the previous two sets of four phrases. In the first set of four phrases, the middle two phrases were specifically located in the Pure Land, whereas now they all pertain to this land.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," each sense organ and the mental faculty are explained individually in relation to each respective gate.
Question:
Why was it stated previously that those with dull faculties are obstructed from hearing the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), whereas here it is said they hear the Gate of Existence?

Answer: Previously one did not enter, but now one enters; because the time for the maturation of the great or small faculties differs, we know that regardless of whether there are obstacles or not, all are able to enter. It is simply a matter of the lightness or heaviness of obstacles being matched against the sharpness or dullness of the faculties, as well as the difference in timing.

If one has not heard either the Great or Small [Vehicles] at all, then regardless of whether there are hindrances or no hindrances, this person lacks the spiritual capacity (*anidhana*) for this land; they have not yet matured in this lifetime and are not included within the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), nor are they subsumed by the four gates. Here, the primary authority is the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (the *Da lun*), specifically the section explaining the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).

It states regarding the fourth power: "By means of this power of wisdom, the World-Honored One thoroughly knows the superior, middling, and inferior faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings. While the treatise discusses only the five faculties such as faith and diligence, as well as the four obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth, in relation to the Small Vehicle;

here, it is applied universally to the Mahāyāna. Therefore, we know that whether there are hindrances or not is of secondary importance; what is valued is simply the presence of faculties and the seeds of the vehicle (*yānagotra*).

The hindrances arising from the violation of precepts are fully detailed in the fourfold analysis of the relationship between the Vehicle and the Precepts; this is precisely why the various categories of analysis—correlating the five periods, the four teachings, and the three grades—are annotated with the phrase "and so forth."
To elaborate on these words, I fear they may have been omitted.

Regarding the question concerning "the five turbidities and the one-way [path]" and so forth: according to the first two sets of four propositions, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna practitioners would not encounter obstacles; however, the present inquiry follows the perspective of those with Mahāyāna faculties who possess obstacles and did not initially hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This refers to the person described in the fourth proposition of the first set of four.

The first three do not constitute obstacles, whereas only the fourth constitutes an obstacle; because this statement does not fully capture the underlying principle, it is said to be "provisional" (*yīwǎng*).
The intent behind the answer is to fully employ the meaning of the fourth phrase from the preceding text.
First, the obstacle is heavy.
Next, from "If they hear" onwards, the faculties are dull.

Since the Buddha has not yet spoken, the former physicians speak of names such as "permanence" and "self," which accord with their calculations; whereas names such as "impermanence" can treat the turbidity. Therefore, this only obstructs the Great [Vehicle] and does not obstruct the Small.

It is like a single type of faculty: because the five turbidities have not been eliminated, one is incapable of hearing the Great [Vehicle]. Upon reaching the Deer Park, one first uses the Small [Vehicle] to treat the turbidities and only thereafter hears the Great. Therefore, if the views are not eliminated, one is incapable of hearing the Eternal; that which calculates the aggregates as being virtuous is precisely what is treated by the four foundations of mindfulness. "Sai" (騃) also means delusion (*moha*).
Therefore, I blame the former physician for exclusively employing improper and habitual methods; this constitutes not knowing how to nurse and not recognizing the medicine.
Not knowing the nature of the illness and so forth constitutes not recognizing the disease.
Not knowing how to open [the channels] and so forth constitutes not knowing the method of administering the medicine.
They do not understand these three methods of the Guestless Physician.

Second, their constant differences are like the quality of milk—good or bad; the lightness or heaviness of delusive views is called the "root source. Because one first cuts them off and later employs them, they are termed "opening" and "prohibiting."
"Bait" refers to food. Because the timing of eating differs, they grasp only at the names of permanence and bliss; therefore, it is said they do not know what is good or evil.
Because their discourse on the self increases their false habits, it is said they do not recognize the source.
Because it does not clarify that the "constant" (nitya) and the "time" (kāla) are distinct, it is said that one does not understand the opening and closing [of the teaching].
Thus, the Sūtra says:

"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had first taught that [the self] is constant, those who receive transformation would have claimed that this Dharma is the same as that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika). Therefore, it says, "If he were merely to praise," and so forth.
The details regarding these two physicians are as recorded in the third fascicle of the *Zhiguan* [Commentary].
(*Fahua Wenju Ji*, Fascicle 5, Part 1)
